newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori will stay firm on hostages - papers.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori will stay firm on hostages - papers.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori plans to stay firm in his government's standoff with Marxist guerrillas holding about 340 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, newspapers said on Saturday.

"He made it clear that it is not within his plans to negotiate with the subversive group," said the daily Gestion, one of several local newspapers whose editors were invited on Friday by Fujimori to a meeting at Government Palace.

The daily Expreso added that Fujimori "emphatically denied the existence of any dialogue or conversation between the (MRTA) terrorist Victor Polay Campos and the Canadian ambassador in Lima, Anthony Vincent, or any representative of the Peruvian government."

Polay, the former MRTA leader, was jailed in 1992. There had been speculation that the government, or released hostage- turned-mediator Vincent, had been secretly meeting Polay to pressure him to persuade his comrades to end the siege.
Polay's release is one of the principal aims of the MRTA unit that has held the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima since Tuesday night.
Fujimori's meeting with the editors was the only known contact he has had with the media since the crisis began.
Fujimori told the editors the only current channel of dialogue between the government and the rebels was Red Cross representative Michel Minning.
He reiterated the position he outlined in a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton that the safety of the hostages was his first priority.
"He explained that, despite the understandable discomforts, the hostages are in a good position," added Expreso.
Finally, according to Gestion, Fujimori called on the Peruvian people and media to unite behind the government in its effort to end the crisis.
